newsitem.title: USA: US trade negotiator backs China WTO entry with caveat.
newsitem.headline: US trade negotiator backs China WTO entry with caveat.

text.p: China should be admitted to the World Trade Organisation, but only after Beijing provides greater access to its own markets, the top U.S. trade negotiator said on Wednesday.

"The administration believes that it is in our interest that China become a member of the WTO," Charlene Barshefsky told a Senate Finance Committee hearing on her nomination for U.S. Trade Representative. She is currently working in an acting capacity in that post.
The timing of China gaining entry to the world body that is dedicated to lowering trade barriers between countries would depend on China, Barshefsky said.

"China's offers thus far have been largely inadequate with respect to market access for goods, services and agriculture, as well as with respect to adherence to the rules," Barshefsky said. "We understand China is again in the process of revising further its offers," she said, adding that she has a team now in China meeting with the Chinese on that issue.
China must resolve U.S. complaints over barriers to agricultural trade before it gains entry to the WTO, Barshefsky said.
The Senate Finance Committee will consider Barshefsky's nomination on Thursday, and if approved, the nomination would then go before the full Senate for a vote.
The committee Thursday will also consider a waiver related to Barshefsky's nomination. The waiver must ultimately be approved by both the House and Senate.

Barshefsky's nomination to the post has been complicated by a law barring anyone from the post if they have represented a foreign government on trade matters. She represented Canadian lumber interests while working as a Washington lawyer.
Senate Finance Committee Chairman William Roth, a Republican from Delaware, said it appeared Barshefsky had strong bipartisan support on the panel.
In light of ongoing efforts on China gaining entry into the WTO, it would be "premature" for the United States to consider permanent Most Favoured Nation trading status for China, Barshefsky said.

"I believe strongly the United States should not take any action to disincentivize China from making the kinds of market access commitments with respect to WTO accession that permanent MFN might provide," she said.

Current U.S.-China textile talks were proceeding "fairly well," Barshefsky said. The United States is concerned about "Chinese circumvention of our textile quotas, and we're concerned also about U.S. textile producer market access into China," she said.

On Japan, Barshefsky said while the U.S. trade deficit with Japan has declined in recent years, she would be on the lookout for any large uptick in Japanese exports to the United States in autos and other sectors.

"I don't yet know what the trend will be but it's something that we want to keep an eye on and we want to be sure if there is any uptick it is not because of either new, or the persistence of old, market access barriers," she said.

It would be difficult for the United States to achieve a free trade agreement with Chile without "fast track" negotiating authority, Barshefsky said. "Fast track" authority would allow the administration to negotiate a trade pact and then return to Congress for an up or down vote on the deal.

"Our ability to deliver on the commitment to Chile is seen, with some justification, as a litmus test for trade expansion and U.S. interest in this hemisphere," Barshefsky said. U.S. exports to Latin America are expected to exceed those to Europe and Japan combined by 2010, she added.

The trade negotiator also favoured a long-term agreement between the United States and Canada on Canadian wheat shipments. She said she was concerned about a recent increase in Canadian wheat and barley shipments to the United States.
